messages.author: d34d025a513c07fc
messages.subject: Re: HTML Shiny
parts:
First, have you been able to get it to run locally in your computer with runApp()? To do this, you may need to put your HTML file in www/index.html, under the top app directory. See http://rstudio.github.com/shiny/tutorial/#html-ui for more on how to structure it.

To have the application be web-accessible, you'll either need to host it on our public beta server by signing up for a beta account here: http://rstudio.github.com/shiny/tutorial/#deployment-web
Or you can set up your own Shiny server, also described on that page. This requires Linux, though.

-Winston

messages.author: ca443e6eaa0e78ed
messages.subject: Re: HTML Shiny
parts:
Hi Matevz,

I don't recommend starting with the HTML style UI, as it is easier to get wrong until you're familiar with Shiny.

That said:

1) You should not copy the jquery.js, shiny.js, and shiny.css files into your own directory--they are served up by the framework itself.
2) Please use the <script> tags exactly as written in the example.
3) Create a directory for your application, put your server.R in there
4) In the application directory, create a www directory, and put your index.html in there (#3 and #4 are covered in the previous link under "Defining an HTML UI")
5) Start an R session and execute the command shiny::runApp("path-to-application-dir")
6) Open up a web browser and point it to http://localhost:8100/

If the page loads but the plots don't show up, I'm guessing you're either using IE9 or earlier, or a less than up to date version of Chrome/Firefox/Safari, in which case you will need to use a later browser. When hosted by Shiny Server, your Shiny app can be accessed by some older versions of browsers, but when served right out of your R session using the Shiny R package alone you are limited to contemporary browsers.

Hope that helps!

messages.author: ca443e6eaa0e78ed
messages.subject: Re: HTML Shiny
parts:
The first part of your question would work fine locally, no problem; but for it to work from our server (glimmer.rstudio.com), your SQL Server would need to be publicly accessible over the internet (which is generally just not a great practice security-wise). Or else, you would have to set up a scheduled task on one of your machines to dump your SQL Server data to a .csv file periodically and upload it to our servers. Then your Shiny app can do read.csv and use the head function to show just the top input$n rows.

But regarding password protection, it is explicitly not supported on our servers right now nor by Shiny Server. There are a couple of options you have if running Linux (including cloud based like Amazon EC2), but if you only have access to Windows servers then we do not currently have an answer for you (but are hoping to later in the year).

By the way, even if just running locally it is very very important that when you form the SQL query string you do it like this:

vws <- sqlQuery(dbConnect, paste("SELECT TOP", as.numeric(input$n), "Datum, Sava, P1, P2, P3 FROM VWS  ORDER BY ID DESC"))

Without the "as.numeric" it would be easy for a malicious user to set input$n to "10 1; DROP TABLE VWS; --" for example, which would cause your whole database table to be erased! (This is called SQL injection and is probably the most common way websites get hacked.)

Let's keep it friendly, everyone! :)

Rook is in the same category as the others. Can easily run out of a single R process (which you can do with Shiny as well, just call runApp() and leave your session alive) but it won't launch multiple R processes and manage them automatically. This is the job of Shiny Server, rApache, RServe, etc. and they all either don't work on Windows or won't launch multiple R processes on Windows. (At least that's my understanding, I don't have much experience with any of these packages except for Shiny.)

It's quite likely we will add Windows (and Mac) support to Shiny Server in the future, we expect there to be significant demand among Windows-only corporate users.

>
> It's quite likely we will add Windows (and Mac) support to Shiny Server in
> the future, we expect there to be significant demand among Windows-only

There are a few things that Windows doesn't do easily. Redis is a bear
to port to Windows because it takes advantage of a UNIX-ism that
allows a forked process to do copy on write, for example. But IIRC
Shiny Server uses Node.js for the "plumbing", and that does run on
Windows.

I've done a few tests with the Windows 8 Pro "Client Hyper-V" with
small Linux server guests. It's not quite as efficient as KVM or Linux
containers on the same laptop, but it's better than VMware Workstation
or VirtualBox. So if you must have a Linux server in a Windows
environment, Hyper-V is probably a viable option.
